title: Onboard an invoice file
prompt: A supplier uploads invoices.csv to Files/landing in a lakehouse. Finance needs a governed, typed table accessible through the SQL analytics endpoint. The original file must remain unchanged. Which implementation meets all requirements?

options.text: Rename invoices.csv to invoices.parquet and move it under Tables.
options.why: Renaming a file does not create Parquet data or a Delta transaction log.

options.text: Create a SQL endpoint view directly over Files/landing/invoices.csv.
options.why: A Files CSV is not an automatically exposed Delta table in the SQL endpoint.

options.text: Read the CSV in Spark, enforce types, and save a managed Delta table while retaining the CSV.
options.why: The raw file stays intact while a typed Delta table becomes available to SQL consumers.

options.text: Create a Files shortcut to the CSV and wait for SQL metadata synchronization.
options.why: A Files shortcut alone does not convert CSV into a SQL-visible Delta table.

explanation: Storage location, file format, and table registration are separate decisions. Preserve the raw artifact and explicitly create the analytical table.

title: Review medallion storage design
prompt: An architecture review proposes separate storage services: OneLake for bronze CSV archives, Lakehouse for silver Delta, and Warehouse for gold. No independent ADLS account is required. Select TWO corrections to the diagram.

options.text: Show OneLake underneath the lakehouse and warehouse storage.
options.why: OneLake is the shared storage foundation, not a bronze-only product.

options.text: Move every gold table to Warehouse because Lakehouse cannot serve gold.
options.why: Gold describes readiness for consumption; it does not mandate Warehouse.

options.text: Keep all lakehouse data as raw CSV because OneLake cannot hold processed tables.
options.why: OneLake can contain processed Delta tables as well as raw files.

options.text: Treat bronze, silver, and gold as logical data-quality stages, independent of the item choice.
options.why: Medallion stages do not map one-to-one to separate storage services.

explanation: A lakehouse can serve multiple medallion stages. Choose the item for workload needs, then place the data-quality stages inside the design.

title: Investigate a row-count discrepancy
prompt: A Delta table has undergone deletes and compaction. A notebook reading it as Delta returns 900 rows, but a generic Parquet reader scanning every file in its table directory returns 1,650. Neither job failed. What is the most defensible explanation?

options.text: The Delta reader uses committed log state; the directory scan can include obsolete physical files.
options.why: Delta selects the active snapshot rather than blindly reading all Parquet files.

options.text: The SQL endpoint permanently truncates every table to 900 rows.
options.why: There is no such row cap; the mismatch is in the read semantics.

options.text: Compaction creates additional current business rows until VACUUM completes.
options.why: Compaction changes physical layout, not the logical current row set.

options.text: The Delta reader automatically removes duplicate business keys on every query.
options.why: Delta does not infer or enforce business-key deduplication on every read.

explanation: A Delta table is data files plus transaction metadata. Read through a Delta-aware engine; a directory is not a reliable definition of current table contents.

title: Recover from an interrupted append
prompt: An append job writes new Parquet files and then crashes before committing the Delta transaction. A reader starts afterward. The goal is to prevent partial ingestion from becoming visible. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The reader must include all newly created files because they already exist in OneLake.
options.why: Physical file existence is not sufficient to publish a Delta table version.

options.text: The reader includes staged files once a log checkpoint is due, even without a committed transaction.
options.why: A checkpoint summarizes committed state; it does not publish uncommitted staged data.

options.text: VACUUM is required before a consistent read can begin.
options.why: Committed snapshot reads do not depend on immediate cleanup of orphan files.

options.text: A Delta-aware reader uses a committed snapshot and excludes the uncommitted append.
options.why: Publication occurs through the validated transaction commit, not the file upload alone.

explanation: Separate writing physical data from committing metadata. A failed staged write need not become a partially visible table update.

title: Plan a transactional row deletion
prompt: A table has deletion vectors disabled. One Parquet file contains 10,000 rows. A Spark DELETE removes one row. The latest Delta query must exclude it, and yesterday's snapshot must remain readable before cleanup. What physical behavior should you expect?

options.text: The original Parquet file is edited in place and its previous contents are lost.
options.why: The copy-on-write path replaces the affected file rather than modifying it in place.

options.text: A replacement file omits the row; the log marks the old file inactive, and retention preserves history.
options.why: The committed snapshot uses the replacement while the old file can support an older version.

options.text: The original file stays current until OPTIMIZE; a SQL view is needed to hide the deleted row.
options.why: The committed DELETE already changes the active Delta snapshot without requiring a SQL view.

options.text: VACUUM immediately removes every file that ever contained that row.
options.why: DELETE and VACUUM are separate operations, and cleanup respects retention.

explanation: The video describes copy-on-write. That example is not universal when deletion vectors are enabled, so the question states the feature setting explicitly.

title: Coordinate concurrent update jobs
prompt: Two jobs update overlapping files in the same Delta table. An analytical Spark job is already reading a snapshot. Select TWO valid expectations.

options.text: The reader switches to each newly committed file mid-query.
options.why: Snapshot isolation keeps a reader on a consistent table state.

options.text: Both updates always commit because ACID eliminates write conflicts.
options.why: Optimistic concurrency control can reject conflicting modifications.

options.text: A conflicting writer can fail validation and require an appropriate retry.
options.why: A conflict is detected rather than published as a corrupt combined state.

options.text: The reader can continue using its consistent snapshot while another job commits.
options.why: Concurrent activity does not require a reader to see a mixture of versions.

explanation: ACID protects table consistency. It does not promise that every pair of concurrent writes will succeed.

title: Control an additive source change
prompt: A daily append adds an optional delivery_method STRING column to an existing Delta table. Existing types must remain unchanged, prior rows must be retained, and unrelated ingestion jobs must not silently accept schema drift. Which change is the most targeted?

options.text: Enable mergeSchema only on this validated append operation.
options.why: Per-write schema evolution adds the new column without enabling broad session-level drift.

options.text: Overwrite the table with overwriteSchema on every daily run.
options.why: An overwrite conflicts with preserving existing rows in an append workflow.

options.text: Run OPTIMIZE with V-Order before appending the new schema.
options.why: Physical file optimization does not authorize an additive schema change.

options.text: Create the additional field only in an endpoint view and append the unchanged extra-column DataFrame.
options.why: An endpoint view does not authorize an incompatible Spark append or store the new incoming attribute.

explanation: Schema evolution is supported but controlled. Validate an additive change and opt in at the narrowest scope; default enforcement is intentional.

title: Audit a historical version
prompt: DESCRIBE HISTORY still lists version 15. However, all old data files required by that version were removed by a previous VACUUM. An auditor requests VERSION AS OF 15. Which response is correct?

options.text: The log can rebuild every deleted data file from its metadata.
options.why: The log records table state; it does not hold the complete deleted row payload.

options.text: Increasing retention today restores the historical files automatically.
options.why: A future policy change does not recreate files already deleted.

options.text: The snapshot cannot be reconstructed from log entries alone; use a retained backup or other recovery source.
options.why: Historical metadata and the referenced physical data must both remain available.

options.text: Run OPTIMIZE so that deleted historical files are regenerated.
options.why: Compaction works on current table data, not missing historical versions.

explanation: A history entry is not proof that its snapshot is readable. Time travel requires sufficient retained transaction metadata and the associated data files.

title: Design a 30-day audit window
prompt: A gold table is updated every day. Auditors require reproducible reads for the last 30 days, and a VACUUM job runs nightly with seven-day retention. Select TWO policy changes needed to support the requirement.

options.text: Set log retention to 30 days but leave the seven-day obsolete-file cleanup unchanged.
options.why: Longer log retention alone cannot recover the physical files removed by the seven-day cleanup.

options.text: Retain obsolete data files for at least the required audit window, with a suitable operational margin.
options.why: A seven-day cleanup can remove data files needed by older audit snapshots.

options.text: Schedule OPTIMIZE more frequently so old versions become permanent.
options.why: Compaction does not replace a retention policy for history.

options.text: Retain sufficient transaction-log history and prevent cleanup jobs from overriding the audit policy.
options.why: Both metadata retention and physical data retention must align with the audit requirement.

explanation: Define the recovery window before cleanup. File retention and log retention are distinct controls; test required historical versions as part of the policy.

title: Evaluate cleanup candidates
prompt: At 12:00 UTC, file A is active and was created 20 days ago; B became obsolete 10 days ago; C became obsolete two days ago; D is active and was created yesterday. No reader needs B. With 168-hour retention, which file is eligible for removal?

options.text: A and B, because both are older than seven days.
options.why: An old file still referenced by the current table is not eligible merely because of its age.

options.text: B only, because it is obsolete and outside the retention interval.
options.why: Eligibility combines being unreferenced with being older than the configured threshold.

options.text: B and C, because obsolete files can be removed immediately.
options.why: C is still within the two-day age and seven-day retention boundary.

options.text: B and D, because VACUUM also rewrites yesterday's active files during cleanup.
options.why: VACUUM does not rewrite or delete the current active file D merely because a cleanup job runs.

explanation: Evaluate current references and the obsolete-file retention threshold. VACUUM is not a command to delete every old Parquet file.

title: Diagnose table-read latency
prompt: A Delta table has 24,000 active two-megabyte files after frequent appends. Queries spend most of their time opening files. Storage cleanup is a secondary concern. Which command directly addresses the primary bottleneck?

options.text: VACUUM dbo.shipments RETAIN 168 HOURS
options.why: VACUUM removes eligible obsolete files; it does not combine active small files.

options.text: SET spark.sql.parquet.vorder.default = TRUE
options.why: A session setting changes future write behavior; it does not compact these existing active files.

options.text: ALTER TABLE dbo.shipments SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.parquet.vorder.enabled'='true')
options.why: A table-level write setting is not an operation combining the already-existing files.

options.text: OPTIMIZE dbo.shipments
options.why: Compaction rewrites active small files into fewer, larger files without changing the current rows.

explanation: Match the operation to the symptom: compaction for file-open overhead, VACUUM for eligible obsolete storage, and V-Order for a read-oriented Parquet layout.

title: Plan a maintenance run
prompt: A read-heavy gold table has small files. The load must finish successfully before optimization. The retention policy is already approved, but deletion candidates must be reviewed before cleanup. Put the four steps in the required order.

options.text: Run VACUUM with the approved retention after candidate review.
options.why: Cleanup is last and must use the approved retention.

options.text: Complete and validate the gold-table ingestion.
options.why: Optimization must operate on the successfully loaded table.

options.text: Run OPTIMIZE with the chosen read-layout optimization.
options.why: Compaction follows the successful load and precedes candidate review.

options.text: Inspect VACUUM DRY RUN results against the retention policy.
options.why: Review the proposed deletions before the deleting command.

explanation: Use success dependencies, not independent schedules that can race ingestion. OPTIMIZE can create obsolete pre-compaction files, but they are not immediately eligible for deletion.

title: Validate a new workspace configuration
prompt: A 2025 tutorial says V-Order is enabled by default. A new workspace created today uses a write-heavy ingestion workload. An engineer wants to assume every newly written file is V-Ordered without checking anything. What is the best recommendation?

options.text: Inspect the actual settings; current documentation disables V-Order by default in new workspaces.
options.why: Workspace/runtime defaults can differ from an older tutorial, and the write-heavy workload matters.

options.text: Assume it is enabled because every OneLake file is V-Ordered.
options.why: OneLake storage does not imply that V-Order is enabled for every writer.

options.text: Enable V-Order globally because it always makes writes faster.
options.why: V-Order is a read optimization that can increase write work.

options.text: Apply V-Order to every bronze write without benchmarking because its write overhead is always exactly 15%.
options.why: The reported average overhead is workload-dependent; blindly optimizing a write-heavy path is unjustified.

explanation: The video's default-setting statement is outdated. Treat default settings as versioned facts and make a workload-based decision, not a memory-based assumption.

title: Apply a read-layout change
prompt: A gold table's existing files are not V-Ordered. You set delta.parquet.vorder.enabled=true for future writes and want to improve reads over the entire existing table. Select TWO valid conclusions.

options.text: The property immediately rewrites all previously created Parquet files.
options.why: Changing a property affects subsequent writing behavior, not a historical file rewrite.

options.text: The table property guarantees V-Order regardless of session-level or writer configuration.
options.why: The table property is one configuration scope; session or write settings can affect effective behavior.

options.text: Existing files retain their previous layout until an operation rewrites them.
options.why: A configuration change alone does not alter physical bytes already stored.

options.text: Use an appropriate OPTIMIZE operation with V-Order to rewrite the existing layout, and measure the result.
options.why: A physical rewrite is needed when the target is the already-existing files.

explanation: Distinguish a setting governing writes from a maintenance operation rewriting files. Query improvements and write overhead depend on the actual workload.

title: Tune bronze and gold writing
prompt: Bronze ingestion has a strict write-latency target. Gold has frequent interactive scans. Both use the same notebook session, whose spark.sql.parquet.vorder.default is false. You need V-Order only for a single gold DataFrame write. Which option is the most targeted?

options.text: Enable the session default before both writes and leave it enabled.
options.why: A session-wide default also affects unrelated bronze writes.

options.text: Set .option('parquet.vorder.enabled','true') on the gold Delta write only.
options.why: A per-write setting targets the required operation while the session default remains false.

options.text: Apply the per-write V-Order option to both bronze and gold for consistent formatting.
options.why: That also adds the unwanted read-layout work to the latency-sensitive bronze write.

options.text: Enable the session setting only after the gold write and assume it retroactively changes the files.
options.why: Changing a setting afterward does not rewrite the gold files that were already produced.

explanation: Use the smallest effective scope. A write-level V-Order option isolates the gold write; confirm precedence if session settings are later changed.

title: Isolate regional ingestion jobs
prompt: A 480-GB table has six equally sized regions. Six pipelines concurrently MERGE separate regions, and each target predicate explicitly restricts its own region. The team has selected Hive-style partitioning to isolate writers. Which key best matches this design?

options.text: order_id, with hundreds of millions of distinct values.
options.why: This creates extreme fragmentation and does not align with the regional writer boundaries.

options.text: amount, because it is a frequently aggregated decimal.
options.why: High cardinality and aggregation alone are not reasons to choose a partition key.

options.text: region, producing roughly 80 GB per partition and matching the write predicates.
options.why: The cardinality and data volume fit the explicitly disjoint regional jobs.

options.text: second_of_ingestion, because more directories always mean more parallelism.
options.why: Tiny time-based partitions can create many small files and do not isolate regional updates.

explanation: Partition values should align with real access or write boundaries, with enough data per partition. Current Fabric guidance emphasizes disjoint writers and considers liquid clustering for read-only layout goals.

title: Estimate partition granularity
prompt: A 240-GB table spans 12 equally sized months and 200 equally represented categories. Every month-category combination is populated uniformly. The proposal partitions by month AND category. Assuming decimal GB, what is the strongest objection?

options.text: It produces 2,400 partitions averaging 0.1 GB; the added granularity risks many small files.
options.why: 240 divided by 12×200 is 0.1 GB per populated combination, before considering incremental writes.

options.text: It produces 212 partitions averaging about 1.13 GB, so the design is automatically optimal.
options.why: Populated combinations multiply; the partition count is not the sum of cardinalities.

options.text: It produces 12 partitions averaging 20 GB because only the first partition column matters.
options.why: Hive-style partitioning includes both keys in the physical hierarchy.

options.text: It cannot be represented because Delta permits only one partition column.
options.why: Delta supports multiple partition columns; the concern is suitability, not syntax.

explanation: Compute the populated combinations, not just the first key's distinct values. Then evaluate typical file size, load patterns, and predicate benefits before adding a second key.

title: Review a regional MERGE condition
prompt: An existing Delta table is partitioned by region. order_id is unique only within a region. Two MERGE jobs process different regions; the EMEA job's source is already filtered to EMEA. It must avoid modifying another region's same-numbered orders and explicitly restrict the target file set. Which ON condition meets both requirements?

options.text: ON t.order_id = s.order_id
options.why: Matching only a region-local identifier can affect another region and leaves the target scope broad.

options.text: ON t.order_id = s.order_id AND s.region = 'EMEA'
options.why: A source-only filter does not restrict the target to the matching region.

options.text: ON t.order_id = s.order_id AND t.region IS NOT NULL
options.why: The target still includes other non-null regions and can match their local order identifiers.

options.text: ON t.order_id = s.order_id AND t.region = s.region AND t.region = 'EMEA'
options.why: The join includes region identity and an explicit constant target partition restriction.

explanation: Partitioning alone does not isolate concurrent MERGE jobs. Include the correct business-key scope and explicit target partition conditions, rather than relying solely on prefiltered inputs.

title: Assess layout-demo results
prompt: The video uses the same few sales rows in three tables: unpartitioned, category-partitioned, and category-region-partitioned. A teammate copies the most partitioned layout into a 700-KB reference table because it must be the fastest. Select TWO appropriate responses.

options.text: Assume the multi-column layout is fastest because it has the most directories.
options.why: More directories are not an unconditional performance improvement.

options.text: Keep the small reference table unpartitioned unless a measured workload justifies a different layout.
options.why: The tiny table cannot meaningfully benefit from many small partitions.

options.text: Explain that partitioning changes physical organization without changing the intended logical row set.
options.why: The demonstrations show layouts of the same data, not different business data.

options.text: Benchmark only the four-row demo and select its fastest single run as the universal production layout.
options.why: A tiny single-run demonstration is not representative evidence for production workload performance.

explanation: The demo teaches a mechanism, not an optimization prescription. Table size and workload constraints decide whether that mechanism is useful.

title: Inspect a partitioned Delta table
prompt: A table is defined USING DELTA PARTITIONED BY (category, region). The populated pairs are (A, EU), (A, US), and (B, EU). Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: The table has a separate transaction log in every populated region folder.
options.why: The table's Delta log governs the table snapshot; partition folders are data layout.

options.text: Region folders always sit at the root, even though category is listed first.
options.why: The specified partition-column order places category above region in the physical hierarchy.

options.text: Every category-region pair shares one physical directory because category is first.
options.why: Each populated combination is represented in the nested partition structure.

options.text: The populated hierarchy includes category=A/region=EU, category=A/region=US, and category=B/region=EU.
options.why: The folder layout represents the existing value combinations in partition-column order.

explanation: Distinguish logical table rows from physical partition paths. Multiple keys create a hierarchy of populated combinations rather than independent tables.

title: Diagnose inconsistent engine visibility
prompt: A team creates a plain shortcut under Files to an S3 folder containing CSV and JSON. Spark can read it, but the SQL analytics endpoint does not list a table. Transformations were not enabled. The team requires no new managed copy and can switch the upstream format to Delta. Which repair best fits?

options.text: Use the complete upstream Delta table root and create a shortcut under Tables.
options.why: The Tables shortcut exposes a suitable Delta table instead of treating raw files as an automatic table.

options.text: Register the external CSV with Spark USING CSV and wait for the endpoint to expose it as Delta.
options.why: Spark registration of CSV does not supply the Delta table required by the stated endpoint pattern.

options.text: Grant SQL UPDATE permission on the Files shortcut.
options.why: Permissions do not convert raw files or enable lakehouse endpoint DML.

options.text: Copy the CSV into Warehouse and keep it synchronized nightly.
options.why: That creates another managed copy and violates the explicit no-copy constraint.

explanation: Shortcut placement and target format matter. A plain Files shortcut is file virtualization, not automatic CSV-to-Delta conversion. Shortcut transformations are a separate capability.

title: Share procurement data across workspaces
prompt: The producer lakehouse contains a procurement schema with 15 Delta tables. A second workspace needs the schema without independent table copies and must reflect source-table changes. Both lakehouses are schema-enabled, required access is already granted, and both Spark and SQL consumers need the tables. What is the most appropriate implementation?

options.text: Create fifteen local tables with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT and refresh them weekly.
options.why: That creates independently stored copies and a separate refresh process.

options.text: Create a schema shortcut from the consumer's Tables section to the producer's procurement schema.
options.why: A schema shortcut references the source tables while presenting the schema in the consumer.

options.text: Create a Files shortcut to exported CSV versions of the producer tables.
options.why: CSV exports are not the requested governed Delta schema representation.

options.text: Create fifteen SQL endpoint views but no consumer lakehouse schema or table references.
options.why: Endpoint-only views do not expose the requested lakehouse schema to the Spark consumers.

explanation: Use the granularity that matches the requirement. A schema shortcut differs from a shortcut to one table and from a copy-based integration.

title: Revise source-retention requirements
prompt: A consumer uses a plain internal shortcut to a producer Delta table. The producer plans to delete the only source table next week. Compliance needs the consumer to retain the data afterward. Which plan satisfies that new requirement?

options.text: Keep the shortcut; its name guarantees an independent retained table.
options.why: The ordinary shortcut references the source instead of creating an independent backup.

options.text: Enable external S3 shortcut caching for the internal shortcut.
options.why: The cited external-cache setting does not turn an internal reference into a durable backup.

options.text: Preserve the source or create an approved independent copy before deletion; keep the shortcut only while its target exists.
options.why: Durable retention requires preserved data, not just a reference to a deleted location.

options.text: Retain only a copy of _delta_log after deleting the producer's data files.
options.why: Transaction metadata alone cannot reconstruct data files that have been deleted.

explanation: A no-copy benefit also creates a source dependency. Revisit the architecture when the requirement changes from live access to independent retention.

title: Forecast remote file reads
prompt: S3 shortcut caching is enabled. A 600-MB file and a 1.4-GB file are read twice; neither source file changes. Both reads occur inside the retention period. Which outcome is consistent with the documented cache rules?

options.text: Both files are eligible because the one-GB threshold is applied only after the whole folder is compressed.
options.why: The documented threshold applies to individual files; folder-level compression is not the eligibility test.

options.text: Only the 1.4-GB file is eligible because one GB is the minimum file size for caching.
options.why: One GB is an upper eligibility boundary, not a minimum for this cache.

options.text: Neither can be cached because shortcuts never store any bytes in OneLake.
options.why: The shortcut cache can temporarily store eligible external file content.

options.text: The second 600-MB read can use cache; the 1.4-GB file remains an external read.
options.why: The smaller file is eligible, while the larger file exceeds the per-file caching limit.

explanation: Plain shortcut semantics and cache implementation are distinct. A shortcut avoids a separately managed full dataset copy, but eligible external content can be cached.

title: Read an updated external file
prompt: A 200-MB file uses an S3 shortcut with a three-day cache-retention setting. It was read yesterday, then updated at the source this morning. It is read again this afternoon. What should OneLake do under the documented behavior?

options.text: Serve the newer source version and update its cache rather than insisting on the old cached bytes.
options.why: OneLake checks the source version and refreshes the cached file when a newer source version exists.

options.text: Serve yesterday's file for exactly three days, regardless of source changes.
options.why: Cache retention is not a guarantee that stale content will be used despite source updates.

options.text: Turn the shortcut into a permanently synchronized standalone table.
options.why: A cache does not become an independently managed mirrored table.

options.text: Reject the read until an administrator resets the cache after every source update.
options.why: The documented source-version check can refresh the cache without requiring a manual reset for every update.

explanation: The inactivity retention and source-version check solve different problems. Re-access also resets the cached file's retention period under the documented policy.

title: Configure external file caching
prompt: A workspace has four plain external shortcut sources: Google Cloud Storage, Amazon S3, ADLS Gen2, and an S3-compatible endpoint. It wants the documented workspace shortcut cache, with eligible sub-1-GB files. Select THREE sources currently supported by that cache feature.

options.text: Google Cloud Storage
options.why: The documented shortcut cache includes GCS.

options.text: Amazon S3
options.why: The documented shortcut cache includes Amazon S3.

options.text: ADLS Gen2
options.why: Being a supported shortcut source does not imply support by this particular cache feature.

options.text: S3-compatible storage
options.why: The documented shortcut cache includes S3-compatible sources.

explanation: Supported shortcut targets and supported shortcut-cache targets are separate lists. Verify the feature-specific list rather than generalizing from connectivity.

title: Reorganize table namespaces
prompt: A schema-enabled lakehouse has dbo.suppliers. The table is moved to procurement.suppliers. Notebook code and SQL queries currently hard-code dbo.suppliers. No data copy is intended. Select TWO conclusions.

options.text: Every existing reference automatically redirects forever, so no dependency work is required.
options.why: A schema move is a namespace change; dependent code may need updates.

options.text: The move means procurement is a physical partition key inside the table.
options.why: A database schema groups tables; it is not a Hive-style partition column.

options.text: Update the references in dependent code and validate downstream consumers.
options.why: Namespace changes require impact analysis and dependency updates.

options.text: Keep schema organization distinct from partition layout and medallion quality stages.
options.why: Schemas, partitions, and processing stages describe different architectural dimensions.

explanation: Organizational changes can break references without changing the business rows. Do not confuse table namespaces with physical partitions.

title: Implement SQL consumption requirements
prompt: An analyst uses the lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint. Required permissions are granted, and a Delta table is synchronized. Select THREE operations available within the endpoint's documented read-only-data boundary.

options.text: SELECT the current Delta table rows.
options.why: Reading synchronized Delta tables is the endpoint's core purpose.

options.text: CREATE VIEW to encapsulate a read query over that table.
options.why: SQL views can be created without inserting or updating underlying Delta data.

options.text: UPDATE the underlying Delta table's amount column.
options.why: Underlying-table DML is not supported through the lakehouse SQL endpoint.

options.text: Create a stored procedure that performs supported SELECT queries only.
options.why: Stored procedures can encapsulate supported read logic; this does not authorize data writes.

explanation: Separate data read-only restrictions from SQL metadata objects. A view or read-only procedure is compatible with the boundary; DML is not.

title: Resolve an object-visibility discrepancy
prompt: An analyst creates reporting.v_supplier in the SQL analytics endpoint. It is queryable in SSMS. A Spark notebook attached to the lakehouse tries to read it as a managed Delta table and cannot find it. Both callers have access. What explains the mismatch?

options.text: The view disappears whenever SSMS disconnects.
options.why: A persisted endpoint view is not simply a client-side session object.

options.text: The view is an endpoint SQL object, not a newly materialized Delta table in the lakehouse catalog.
options.why: Creating the view does not write a corresponding managed Delta table for Spark.

options.text: V-Order must be enabled before Spark can resolve any SQL view.
options.why: Parquet layout settings do not reconcile SQL and Spark object catalogs.

options.text: The endpoint's next metadata synchronization will automatically materialize the view as a Spark Delta table.
options.why: SQL object synchronization does not imply physical materialization of a view into a Spark-managed Delta table.

explanation: A SQL endpoint's logical view and a physical Delta table have different lifecycles and visibility. Materialize deliberately if a physical shared table is required.

title: Connect an external SQL client
prompt: An external application needs SELECT access to a lakehouse using T-SQL and the TDS protocol. Its developer already has the OneLake ABFSS path and assumes that is the database server name. What should the developer use instead?

options.text: The Files path, with .csv appended to the table name.
options.why: A file path is not a TDS database connection endpoint.

options.text: The Spark application ID as the SQL server address.
options.why: A Spark job identifier is not a SQL analytics connection string.

options.text: The SQL analytics endpoint connection string from the item settings, using the required identity and permissions.
options.why: The intended T-SQL/TDS workload connects through the SQL endpoint rather than a storage URI.

options.text: The OneLake DFS host as the TDS server and the workspace name as the SQL database.
options.why: OneLake DFS is a storage interface; it is not interchangeable with the SQL/TDS endpoint.

explanation: Choose the interface for the task: OneLake/ABFSS for storage-aware access, Spark for data engineering, and the SQL endpoint for supported T-SQL reads.

title: Update reference material
prompt: A business user uses OneLake file explorer. They need to upload an updated raw reference CSV and correct one value in a governed Delta table. Select TWO appropriate actions.

options.text: Edit an arbitrary active Parquet file directly and leave _delta_log unchanged.
options.why: Direct file mutation bypasses Delta's transaction metadata and can corrupt table consistency.

options.text: Upload the raw CSV to the intended Files folder through the supported file tool.
options.why: Raw file management is a suitable use of the explorer.

options.text: Use an authorized Delta-aware Spark operation for the table-row correction.
options.why: The table change must be committed through the table's transactional write path.

options.text: Use an UPDATE through the lakehouse SQL endpoint because the user can already SELECT the table.
options.why: SELECT permission does not add unsupported lakehouse endpoint data-writing operations.

explanation: Respect the abstraction boundary. A supported file-management tool can move raw artifacts; editing table internals is not a substitute for a Delta transaction.

title: Investigate cross-capacity reads
prompt: A producer's OneLake data is referenced through an internal shortcut in a consumer workspace on another active capacity. The producer capacity is paused, and the consumer continues to query the shortcut. Which explanation best matches current documented OneLake consumption behavior?

options.text: This can occur because shortcut consumption is counted against the consumer's active capacity.
options.why: Current documentation explicitly distinguishes shortcut consumption from direct transactions on a paused capacity.

options.text: The consumer must be seeing an external cached copy and cannot read updated source data until the producer resumes.
options.why: This is an internal shortcut; the documented active-consumer consumption rule does not require that external-cache explanation.

options.text: Every OneLake request is free when the producer is paused.
options.why: Consumer transactions and continued stored-data billing are not eliminated by pausing the producer.

options.text: The existence of any shortcut makes every direct producer-capacity transaction available while paused.
options.why: The documented shortcut-consumption exception does not unblock every direct request to the paused capacity.

explanation: The video gives a simplified capacity rule. Direct transactions on a paused capacity are rejected; the documented shortcut-consumer-capacity exception matters in a multi-capacity design.

title: Design data access for three teams
prompt: A supported Azure SQL operational database needs a continuously updated analytical copy in OneLake. Three teams in separate workspaces need the same data without three independently managed replication processes. Select TWO components of the best design.

options.text: Create one ordinary shortcut directly to the operational database engine and rely on it for CDC.
options.why: A plain storage shortcut is not database change replication from Azure SQL.

options.text: Create one central Database Mirroring item for the supported operational source.
options.why: A central replication process supplies the analytical Delta copy.

options.text: Create three independent mirrors, because cross-workspace shortcuts always require copies.
options.why: Cross-workspace shortcuts can reference the centrally mirrored data.

options.text: Create authorized consumer shortcuts to the central mirrored tables.
options.why: The teams share the same analytical replica rather than replicating the operational source repeatedly.

explanation: Database replication and reference-based consumption can be combined. First satisfy the external-source replication requirement, then avoid additional team-owned replicas.

title: Evaluate an external catalog integration
prompt: An external open-format catalog is exposed through Metadata Mirroring, which synchronizes its catalog and uses shortcuts. A design review claims this necessarily creates a full replicated Delta copy, just like Database Mirroring of Azure SQL. Which correction is best?

options.text: Metadata Mirroring creates an independent operational SQL database in the consumer for every catalog.
options.why: Synchronizing catalog metadata and referencing open-format data is not creation of an independent operational database.

options.text: Every supported mirroring type always copies every physical data file.
options.why: The mechanism differs between database replication and metadata mirroring.

options.text: The actual data-access mechanism depends on mirroring type and source; this design references data in place.
options.why: Metadata mirroring can use shortcuts while database mirroring continuously replicates data.

options.text: A copied catalog always requires a separate full data-movement Pipeline before any referenced table can be queried.
options.why: The stated shortcut-based mechanism makes supported source data available in place without that obligatory full copy.

explanation: Read the mechanism, not only the product name. The video's shortcut concepts help explain metadata mirroring, but this item extends beyond the video's specific demonstration.

title: Coordinate preparation and quality checks
prompt: A SharePoint Excel source needs Trim, type conversion, and Unpivot with Power Query. After loading a lakehouse, a Notebook quality check must succeed before downstream SQL runs. Select TWO tools and roles that satisfy this workflow.

options.text: Dataflow Gen2 for the Power Query transformations and loading.
options.why: It supplies the requested transformation experience and a supported destination.

options.text: A plain Shortcut to replace all Power Query transformations.
options.why: A reference alone is not the specified transformation recipe.

options.text: A standalone scheduled Dataflow refresh to control the Notebook and SQL success dependencies as well.
options.why: Data preparation does not replace orchestration of the separate Notebook and SQL activities.

options.text: A Pipeline to sequence the Dataflow, Notebook check, and SQL with success dependencies.
options.why: Orchestration must control the heterogeneous activities and their outcomes.

explanation: Transformation and orchestration are complementary. A file upload alone also does not establish a recurring source connection.

title: Design a recurring incremental load
prompt: A source supported by Copy Job needs a recurring direct load with native incremental tracking. There are no Notebook, branching, or cross-activity dependencies. The team wants the least operational complexity. Which choice best meets the stated scope?

options.text: A multi-stage Pipeline with custom incremental state and extra activities.
options.why: It can work, but adds operational complexity absent from the requirements.

options.text: A manual export whenever the analytical table looks outdated.
options.why: That does not meet recurring incremental ingestion requirements.

options.text: An Eventstream to scan the source as a scheduled batch job.
options.why: The stated need is a recurring direct load, not an event stream.

options.text: A Copy Job configured for the supported source and the required incremental behavior.
options.why: Native incremental loading avoids building an unnecessary heterogeneous orchestration flow.

explanation: A Pipeline is justified by orchestration requirements, not merely by the existence of a source and a destination. Verify source-specific support before choosing native incremental behavior.

title: Implement analytical SQL processing
prompt: A BI team has clean relational data and existing T-SQL transformation procedures. It must INSERT, UPDATE, and commit changes spanning multiple tables in an analytical store. Files and Spark notebooks are not required. Which option is most appropriate?

options.text: Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint, because SELECT support implies full DML support.
options.why: The lakehouse endpoint is read-only over its underlying Delta tables.

options.text: Fabric Warehouse, because the requirements center on analytical T-SQL writing and transactions.
options.why: The store matches the relational SQL workflow and transaction requirements.

options.text: Eventhouse, after replacing the team's writing procedures with read-only KQL queries.
options.why: Replacing writing procedures with reads drops the explicit SQL-writing and transaction requirements.

options.text: A Files shortcut, because references provide multi-table transaction handling.
options.why: A storage reference is not a transactional analytical SQL store.

explanation: Do not confuse storage format with the operations available through a chosen surface. Lakehouse and Warehouse can share OneLake while offering different write workflows.

title: Process mixed source artifacts
prompt: An engineering team must preserve source JSON, CSV, and inspection images, use PySpark to build standardized Delta tables, and expose the resulting tables to SQL analysts. It wants one suitable primary data-engineering item. Which design is best?

options.text: Keep every artifact inside a SQL endpoint view and update it with T-SQL.
options.why: Views do not provide raw-artifact storage, and endpoint DML is not supported.

options.text: Use Warehouse only and port all PySpark transformations to T-SQL while loading raw artifacts into SQL tables.
options.why: This changes the required Spark workflow and raw-artifact handling instead of matching the given data-engineering needs.

options.text: Use a Lakehouse Files area for originals, Spark for transformation, and registered Delta tables for SQL consumption.
options.why: The item supports raw files, Spark engineering, and a SQL read surface for the resulting tables.

options.text: Put a Shortcut on a raw CSV and treat it as a fully prepared typed SQL table.
options.why: Plain file virtualization does not perform the required standardization and Delta-table creation.

explanation: Combine storage and interfaces instead of expecting one interface to do every job. Original artifacts remain distinct from typed analytical tables.

title: Design an IoT analytics path
prompt: A supported IoT source emits continuous events. The solution must filter events before routing and retain them for KQL time-series analysis. Select TWO complementary components.

options.text: Eventstream for continuous ingestion, supported transformations, and routing.
options.why: It supplies the live event-processing path.

options.text: Pipeline Copy activities every 15 minutes instead of a continuously running event-processing path.
options.why: Periodic batch copies do not satisfy the stated continuous event filtering and routing path.

options.text: A SQL endpoint view as the durable event store.
options.why: A logical read view is not the required event storage and KQL engine.

options.text: Eventhouse with a KQL database for event retention and analysis.
options.why: It supplies storage and the requested time-series query surface.

explanation: An ingestion path and an analytical destination solve different requirements. The practical pattern can combine Eventstream and Eventhouse.

title: Extend an existing event pipeline
prompt: A plant already has a working Eventstream. Operations now need to keep a large event history, search semi-structured logs, and run KQL time-window queries. What is the next most appropriate component?

options.text: A second Eventstream that has no analytical destination.
options.why: Another transport path does not provide the required durable query store.

options.text: An Eventhouse KQL database configured as a supported destination.
options.why: It supplies the event-history and KQL analysis capability missing from the current design.

options.text: A Warehouse with the required KQL queries rewritten into T-SQL.
options.why: Changing the query language does not satisfy the specified KQL analysis requirement.

options.text: A Lakehouse Delta table queried through its SQL endpoint, without any KQL database.
options.why: This supplies a SQL table surface but not the required KQL analytical component.

explanation: Find the missing capability before adding another tool. The stream moves events; the destination must retain and analyze them.
